extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political economy; interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and argumentative principles about the justice, nature, and social effects of loans, interest, capital formation, and leisure in a market economy. The text uses illustrative stories (house, plane) to derive practical rules and policy implications for lending and saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for fair temporary use of another's property
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person occupies another's house for a year, the occupier must (1) quit at the end of the year and restore the house in good repair save natural decay, (2) refund architect/maintenance costs the owner pays while the house was in service, and (3) render a service equivalent to what he receives; equivalence is to be freely discussed between parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a judges' decision in the house anecdote; emphasises free agreement, restitution for wear, and compensation for services received as the basis of justice in temporary transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration when lending tools or instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: When an instrument of labour (the plane) is lent, the lender is entitled to remuneration calculated so that at the end of the term he recovers an equivalent instrument (or funds to replace/repair it) plus compensation for the advantage he gave up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: James demands a payment so that after one year he has the plane like new and compensation (a new plank) for the benefit he relinquished. The arrangement is depicted as neither oppressive nor unjust when freely agreed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest is natural, lawful, and just
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest is the legitimate remuneration of capital: capital (instruments, provisions) increases productive power and was prepared by labour, so it is just that it yield an advantage to its possessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from the producer's investment of time, skill and strength; denies that interest is inherently oppression and compares it to remuneration for any other service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary consent limits harm from loans
rubrics_metrics.description: A loan entered into freely cannot injure the borrower: if the remuneration demanded is excessive, the borrower will refuse; by borrowing he signals that the advantages (after remuneration) outweigh inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges errors of judgment or coercive necessity can make borrowing harmful, but treats these as accidental problems rather than condemnations of the institution of interest itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply and demand determine remuneration (interest rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate of remuneration for loans is set by the same law that governs the equivalent of all services — supply and demand. Abundance of capital lowers interest; scarcity raises it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses intuitive examples (water in Pyrenees vs Sahara) and historical interest-rate declines to explain why abundance reduces the relative service a lender provides and thus reduces interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity/duration of interest is explicable and legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: A capital good can be lent repeatedly, producing a perpetual stream of interest so long as wear is accounted for and the lender regains equivalent value at each term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how repeated lending yields perpetual interest, how wear is borne by the borrower in calculation, and how multiple successive loans rest on the same principle as the first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash is a transient form of value; lending money equals lending productive value
rubrics_metrics.description: Money is merely a transient medium used to obtain real instruments or provisions; lending cash is economically equivalent to lending tools because it enables the borrower to obtain productive means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counters the objection that money cannot reproduce itself by showing that money is used to acquire instruments that increase productivity and thus justify remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishing interest (gratuitous credit) would destroy the incentive to save
rubrics_metrics.description: If interest were annihilated, there would be no motive for saving or preserving capital; waste and scarcity would follow and interest would inevitably reappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets doctrines (e.g., Proudhon's claim) that social perfection implies gratuitous credit; argues such claims are sophistry and dangerous because they undermine capital formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depression of interest benefits borrowers and consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower interest (resulting from abundant capital) primarily benefits borrowers and, ultimately, consumers by reducing costs and promoting production; thus declining interest helps the proletariat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that as capital becomes more abundant, interest falls, improving conditions for those who borrow to operate on materials and instruments; historical examples cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workers should favour conditions that promote saving and capital formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who operate on materials and instruments (the 'prolétaires') have a direct interest in laws and customs that encourage saving and capital accumulation (peace, order, security, low public expense, simplicity), because that increases availability of capital and lowers borrowing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists policy and cultural conditions favourable to saving; frames it as practical self-interest for workers rather than abstract philanthropy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of capital causes low wages (effect), not the reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Low wages are presented as an effect of scarce capital (and consequent competition for subsistence), not the cause of scarcity; scarcity allows capital-holders to 'auction' labour on harsh terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses thought experiments about a small population with very few capitalists to show how scarcity concentrates market power and produces dire outcomes for most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insecurity and political disturbance raise interest and harm workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Political upheaval (e.g., the revolution of February) undermines business confidence, discourages saving, raises interest rates, reduces access to materials and instruments for workers, and causes stoppages that lower wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws a causal link from insecurity to capital flight/scarcity and then to higher interest and worse conditions for the labouring classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure as lawful fruit of past activity and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure that results lawfully from past labour and saving is legitimate and socially beneficial (enables scientific and artistic progress); it is not necessarily the result of plunder and can be an innocent reward of productive activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes lawful leisure from leisure gained by oppression; claims leisure enables inventions, arts and sciences, and has moral and cultural value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition among lenders restrains exploitative demands
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of many lenders or many capital goods constrains any single lender from demanding exorbitant remuneration because borrowers can choose alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that absence of rivalry is the most favourable circumstance for maximal requisitions by a lender; therefore abundance is protective for borrowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loans do not create borrowers' pre-existing necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: If a borrower is forced by prior necessity to accept harsh loan terms, that necessity pre-existed the loan; the loan relieves rather than creates the need and cannot be held wholly responsible for the underlying condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges moral culpability of exploitative lenders but insists economically the loan is not the cause of the borrower’s prior desperate situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual pursuit of advantage produces social harmony rather than irreconcilable class antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: The private efforts of landowners, manufacturers, capitalists and workers — each seeking their own advantage — tend to produce abundance, lower prices, and mutual benefits: the final result of each class's efforts is the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the doctrine of inherent class antagonism, presenting economic interdependence and market processes as a chain of causes producing beneficial outcomes for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject jealousies and class hatreds as economically harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy, ill-will and unfounded hatred between classes injure those who hold them and are unnecessary because economic laws demonstrate mutual benefits; such passions are not constructive economic policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral admonition tied to economic argumentation: hatred and suspicion damage social harmony and retard the formation and circulation of capital.
